Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:19: In the Talmud (Berachot 24b), chapter "One Whose Dead," Rav Huna said: a Torah scholar is forbidden to stand in a filthy place, since it is impossible for him to be without Torah [thoughts]. Rabbi Yochanan said, it is permitted to think Torah thoughts anywhere except the bathhouse and the privy. It is taught: a person should not walk through filthy alleyways and place his hand over his mouth and recite the Shema; and not only this, but if he was reciting and came [to such a place], he should stop. If he did not stop, what then? Rabbi Miyasha the grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, of him Scripture says (Ezekiel 20:25) "and I also gave them statutes that were not good," etc. Rav Adda bar Matna said, [of him it is written] (Numbers 15:31) "for he has despised the word of the Lord and has broken His commandment." Rav said, [of him it is written] (Isaiah 5:18) "woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity." If he stopped, what then? Rabbi Abbahu said, of him Scripture says (Deuteronomy 32:47) "and through this matter you shall lengthen your days" - so far. Rashi explains, concerning Rav who said "woe to those who draw iniquity," that it is the way of most people in the world to commit transgressions for their own benefit, whereas this one commits a transgression gratuitously, since he thinks he is performing a mitzvah by reciting [in that place], yet he commits a transgression by demeaning the Torah with that recitation - therefore, "woe to those who draw iniquity" for nothing - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:20: In Sefer Chasidim (siman 949), it is written that in the privy a person should think about his expenses and the household's needed expenses. And Rabbeinu Yonah writes in Sefer HaYirah that he should accustom himself to [such] calculations there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:21: Further, one must be careful of the honor of the Name, that the Name of Heaven not be profaned through him, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Yoma 86a) - their words: our Rabbis taught, when a person reads Scripture and studies Mishnah and attends upon Torah scholars, and his speech is gentle with people, and his business dealings in the marketplace are pleasant, and he does business honestly, what do people say about him? "Happy is so-and-so's father who taught him Torah, happy is his teacher who taught him Torah; woe to those who have not learned Torah - so-and-so learned Torah, see how pleasant his ways are, how proper his deeds" - of him Scripture says (Isaiah 49:3) "and He said to me, you are My servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified." But when a person reads Scripture and studies Mishnah, yet his speech is not gentle with people, and his business dealings in the marketplace are not pleasant, and he does not do business honestly, what do people say about him? "Woe to so-and-so who learned Torah, woe to his father and his teacher who taught him Torah; happy are those who have not learned Torah - so-and-so learned Torah, see how ugly his deeds are, how corrupt his ways" - of him Scripture says (Ezekiel 36:20) "when it was said of them, these are the people of the Lord, and yet they have gone out of His land."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:22: Further, they say there: what is an example of profaning the Name? Rav said, such as I, who take meat from the butcher and do not pay for it immediately. Rabbi Yochanan said, such as I, who walk four cubits without Torah and without tefillin. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said, such as when people say, "may his Master forgive so-and-so." Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi said, such as when his colleagues are ashamed of a teaching reported in his name - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:23: It is already known how strict our Sages, of blessed memory, were about the profanation of the Name; it says there: but whoever has committed a profanation of the Name, repentance has no power to suspend [the punishment], nor does Yom Kippur have power to atone, nor do sufferings have power to cleanse - rather, all of them together suspend it, and death cleanses, as it is said (Isaiah 22:14) "and it was revealed in my ears by the Lord of hosts, surely this iniquity shall not be atoned for you until you die" - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:24: In the Zohar (Pinchas 231a), it says that the first to be judged on Rosh Hashanah is whoever is not careful of the honor of the Lord, as it is said (Job 1:6) "and the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord" - his words: "the first judgment of all is upon whoever does not honor the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, and does not honor the Torah and its servants; likewise, whoever does not take care that the holy Name not be profaned on earth" - so far. And they say, of blessed memory (Vayikra Rabbah 22:6), we find that the Holy One, blessed be He, overlooked idolatry but did not overlook the profanation of the Name, as it is said (Ezekiel 20:39) "and you, house of Israel, thus says the Lord God, go, serve everyone his idols, but My holy Name you shall no longer profane" - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:25: Concerning the matter of profaning the Name, I have chosen to copy the words of the pious Rabbi Yosef Yaavetz, peace be upon him, on the Mishnah (Avot 4:4) "whoever profanes the Name of Heaven in secret" - and the end of the Mishnah's text is, "is punished for it in the open, whether committed unintentionally or deliberately, [both alike] in the profanation of the Name." Rabbi Yehudah ibn Shoshan explains: "whether unintentional or deliberate" is a reason in its own right - just as secret and open are equal in the profanation of the Name, so are the unintentional and the deliberate. The reason is that for one who transgresses the King's command there is a difference between transgressing in secret or in the open, but one who lays a hand on the King Himself - it is all the same; and if we were to judge, it would be fitting to punish the secret [transgression] more than the open, for one who raises a hand against the King before his officers and princes - his foolishness saves him [i.e., he could not have really thought he would get away with it], but in secret he has no merit at all. And likewise the matter of unintentional and deliberate: every person is obligated to write on the tablet of his heart that there is a King who rules over everything, and that it is fitting to fear Him and tremble at His honor, and whoever transgresses this, his blood is on his own head - could a person say to the king, "I forgot and struck you, I forgot and cursed you"? - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:26: The above-mentioned pious one further writes that included in the profanation of the Name of Heaven in secret is one who speaks slander of his fellow in secret, for this transgresses idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said that slander is graver than all of them; proof of this is the matter of Miriam, who spoke slander in secret and unintentionally, and was punished in the open - "and the people did not journey until Miriam was gathered in" - as our Sages, of blessed memory, explain, so that all would know the punishment for slander - so far the sum of his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:27: The second aspect concerning honor is what is written concerning Eli's sons (I Samuel 2:29) "why do you scorn My sacrifice and My offering... and honor your sons above Me, to fatten yourselves with the choicest of every offering of My people Israel?" It appears that one must be careful not to honor any man or woman before honoring the Holy One, blessed be He, similar to what our Sages, of blessed memory, say (Berachot 14a), that it is forbidden to greet one's fellow before praying in the morning at his door; and therefore the Torah commanded that the first of everything be given to the priest, who is the Lord's portion - whether in the matter of the challah offering, called "first," or in the matter of the terumah offerings, and likewise the first fruits.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:28: Further, a second aspect: "and honor your sons above Me" - one must be careful not to honor any person such that his honor exceeds the honor of the Omnipresent, as our Sages, of blessed memory, say (Kiddushin 33b) concerning a certain student sitting before his teacher: Rabbi Abbahu said, a Torah scholar may stand before his teacher only in the morning and evening, so that his honor not exceed the honor of Heaven - so far. And the Rambam, peace be upon him (Laws of Torah Study, chapter 6, halacha 8) rules the law according to Rabbi Abbahu; and although the Rosh and the Rif hold that the law does not follow Rabbi Abbahu, since the honor of a Torah scholar is equal to the honor of the Omnipresent - "you shall fear the Lord your God" including Torah scholars - nevertheless, this is relevant regarding other people, that it is not fitting to stand before them or honor them more than the honor of the Omnipresent.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:29: Further, there is another aspect encompassing all the mitzvot, and it is to honor the Omnipresent just as one honors those human beings whom he is obligated to honor, such as kings and dignitaries; this is what is meant by "and honor your sons above Me" - meaning, would that we were equal, but you have honored them more than Me - and this is along the lines of what our Sages, of blessed memory, say (Berachot 28b), "let the fear of Heaven be upon you like the fear of flesh and blood" - likewise, let the honor of Heaven be upon you like the honor of flesh and blood; and this is a middling measure, but it is really fitting to honor the Holy One, blessed be He, more than human beings, along the lines of "honor the Lord with your wealth" (Proverbs 3:9), which Rabbeinu Yonah, peace be upon him, explains as "more than your wealth" (see Sefer Chasidim, siman 275). For it is known that if an earthly king were to command someone some mitzvah, how carefully he would perform it, with heart and soul, for the honor of the king - likewise he should honor his Maker. Chovot HaLevavot elaborates on this aspect in the Gate of Self-Reckoning, the tenth reckoning, see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:30: Our Sages, of blessed memory, say in Midrash Shmuel (portion 12), concerning the matter of the Ark that was in the Philistine camp for six months, that the Holy One, blessed be He, complained about Israel over this - their words: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said, the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: if one of your chickens were lost, would you not search through several alleyways until you brought it back, yet My Ark wanders in the field of the Philistines and you are not concerned about it? "His right hand and His holy arm brought Him salvation" [i.e., He redeemed it Himself] - so far. This is the matter we explained, that one must be careful about the honor of the Omnipresent as with the honor of flesh and blood.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:31: Further, another branch grows from this, namely to be careful about the honor of his soul more than the honor of his body; and we find that the soul is called "kavod" [glory], since the soul is a portion of Him, blessed be He - whoever honors it through Torah and the repair of the mitzvot and good deeds honors the Holy One, blessed be He - while the body, created from a putrid drop, is a portion of this world, a portion of humanity, and the body ultimately perishes and is lost, just as all the goods of this world will ultimately be destroyed and consumed, because they stem from the skin of the serpent and its kelipah. We find, then, that one who honors his body more than his soul is like one who honors human beings more than the Holy One, blessed be He; therefore he should be careful about the honor of his soul more than the honor of his body, and not give priority to his body but first attend to the honor of his soul and only afterward his body, as our Sages, of blessed memory, say (Berachot 10b), that it is forbidden to eat before praying; and in the Zohar (Beshalach 62b), it likewise says that before eating one should occupy himself with Torah, as it is said (Proverbs 13:25) "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" - after his soul is satisfied with Torah and prayer; and this is what is meant by "to fatten yourselves with the choicest of every," etc., as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:32: Similarly in all matters, one should not give priority to his own affairs over the affairs of Heaven. The example: if he is a craftsman, let him divide his day, half for his craft and half to occupy himself with Torah, so that the honor of his body equal the honor of his soul; and before engaging in his craft, let him occupy himself with Torah, to give priority to his soul, so that Torah be primary and craft secondary, and by this merit he will succeed in his craft, as our Sages, of blessed memory, explain (Avodah Zarah 19b), that this matter is written in the Torah, that one who occupies himself with Torah, his possessions succeed - on condition that he give priority to Torah over craft, as I explained; and so the verses prove: (Psalms 1:2) "but his delight is in the Torah of the Lord," etc., and afterward, "and whatever he does shall prosper" - and so the other verses prove. But if he gives priority to his own affairs over the affairs of Heaven, he will come to be idle from Torah, as it is said (Avot 4:10), "if you have neglected Torah, you will have many neglecters against you" - and this matter has been tested by many.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:33: Likewise, from all the worldly matters in which a person honors himself, he should take a proof to honor his soul; this is what our Sages, of blessed memory, say in the midrash (Yalkut Mishlei, remez 932), on the verse (Proverbs 2:4) "if you seek her as silver" - their words: Scripture tells us that just as a person is careful of his coin, that it not be lost, so he must be careful of his learning, that it not be lost; and just as silver is hard to acquire, so are words of Torah hard to acquire - but is it that just as silver is hard to lose, so are words of Torah? The verse teaches (Job 28:17) "gold and glass cannot equal it" - hard to acquire like gold, and easy to lose like a glass vessel - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:34: Along these lines, they say there on this verse: Reish Lakish said, if a person does not go after words of Torah, they do not come after him. Likewise (Avot 4:14), Rabbi Nehorai says, "exile yourself to a place of Torah." And if a person searches after them, through this he merits wisdom and understanding, as it is said (Proverbs 2:5) "and you shall find the knowledge of God" - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:35: We find, then, that just as a person honors his body by pursuing silver and gold - and if he were told, "go to such-and-such a place and there you will profit so much money," he would not neglect to strive with diligence and alacrity - so should he strive with diligence and alacrity after the honor of Torah, which is the honor of his soul, for there is no honor in the World to Come except Torah, as it is said (ibid. 3:35) "the wise shall inherit honor."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:36: Likewise, just as he honors his body with fine garments, he should repair his soul with beautiful mitzvot - a beautiful tallit, beautiful tefillin - as our Sages, of blessed memory, say (Exodus 15:2) "this is my God and I will glorify Him" - beautify yourself before Him through the commandments. In Tractate Shabbat, chapter Rabbi Eliezer of Circumcision (133b): "this is my God and I will glorify Him" - beautify yourself before Him through the commandments: make a beautiful sukkah, a beautiful lulav, a beautiful shofar, write a Torah scroll for its own sake with beautiful ink, with a beautiful quill, by a skilled scribe, and wrap it in beautiful silks. Abba Shaul says, be like Him: just as He is merciful and gracious, so you be merciful and gracious - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:37: There is yet another aspect close to what we have written, namely what our Sages, of blessed memory, say (Shabbat 113a), that Rabbi Yochanan would call his garments "my honorers" [mechabdotai]. From this we may extend the analogy to the matter of the soul: just as the body is honored among people when its garments are fine, without stains and the like, so the soul is honored in the World to Come only through its garment, which is the limbs of the body, when they are beautiful through the repair of the mitzvot, and are likewise beautiful without the stains of sin and without any blemish - through this, honor comes to the soul; but if any of these is lacking, there is no honor for the soul. To this the Tikkunim allude (22b), saying "beautiful vessels for its limbs" - for just as a person needs beautiful vessels to clothe himself, so his limbs, which are the garment of his soul, need to be beautiful in the conditions I explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:38: The third aspect is that one should not regard himself as important in a place where the honor of the Lord is present. Proof of this is in the matter of David, when Michal, Saul's daughter, rebuked him, saying to him (II Samuel 6:20) "how honored the king of Israel was today, who uncovered himself today before the eyes of his servants' maidservants, as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!" And David the king, peace be upon him, answered (ibid. 6:22) "and I will be still more lightly esteemed than this, and will be lowly in my own eyes," etc. Our Sages, of blessed memory, say in the Sifrei - their words: she said to him, "my father's house was more dignified than you - God forbid that their palm or sole or heel should ever have been seen uncovered, but they were all more honored than you." And in Midrash Rabbah, portion of Bemidbar (4:20), it says: they were modest and holy. And what did David say? "Before the Lord, who chose me," etc. - your father's house sought their own honor and neglected the honor of Heaven, but I do not do so; rather, I set aside my own honor and seek the honor of Heaven - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:39: Now, Michal, Saul's daughter, rebuked David the king, peace be upon him, as would seem reasonable by intellect - that the honor of the Lord should not be [manifested] by making oneself lightly esteemed, dancing and whirling, so that he necessarily exposes himself, and that the honor of the Lord requires that a person conduct himself with gravity of demeanor. David answered her that since the honor of the Lord cannot be less than this [display], I set aside my own honor and seek the honor of Heaven - and by saying "seek," he means that he seeks that everyone see the honor of Heaven, and had he walked with gravity of demeanor, the honor of Heaven would not have been seen by all.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:40: We thus learn a fourth aspect concerning the honor of the Lord: that sometimes one must be careful of the honor of the Lord by maintaining gravity of demeanor, such as while standing in prayer and the like - this is the explanation of the word "kavod" [honor], from the language of "heaviness" [koved] - proof being "and he who is lightly esteemed shall be honored" [an implied contrast].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:41: But when it is a time of joy, to gladden the Omnipresent, the honor of the Lord is shown by making oneself light, dancing and whirling; along these lines we find Aaron the priest, whom the Lord commanded (Leviticus 6:3) "and he shall remove the ashes," despite all his greatness, and likewise Elazar son of Aaron, of whom it is said (Numbers 4:16) "and the appointed duty of Elazar son of Aaron the priest is the oil for the light, the incense of spices, the daily grain offering, and the anointing oil," etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:42: In Midrash Rabbah (Bemidbar Rabbah 4:20), on the explanation of this verse, our Sages, of blessed memory, say: "'and the appointed duty of Elazar son of Aaron the priest,' etc. - this is [the meaning of] (Proverbs 25:6) 'do not glorify yourself before the king, and do not stand in the place of great men' - if before an earthly king a person must conduct himself with lowliness, how much more so before the Omnipresent; and we learn, 'be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer, and mighty as a lion, to do the will of your Father in Heaven' - to teach you that there is no pride before the Omnipresent. Elijah says: whoever increases the honor of Heaven and diminishes his own honor, the honor of Heaven increases and his own honor increases; and whoever diminishes the honor of Heaven and increases his own honor, the honor of Heaven remains in its place and his own honor diminishes." A story is told of a certain man, etc. - two stories are brought there, which we have already quoted from the passage of Tanna DeVei Eliyahu in the Gate of Fear, chapter 4, which brought these stories.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:43: It says there in Midrash Rabbah, after the aforementioned stories: from this you learn that a person should not conduct himself with pride before the Omnipresent, for whoever is proud before Him is demeaned, as it is said (I Samuel 2:30) "for those who honor Me I will honor, and those who demean Me shall be treated with contempt." And so you find with David, King of Israel, that he did not conduct himself with pride before the Omnipresent, but demeaned himself before Him like a commoner, to increase the honor of the Omnipresent. When was this? At the time he brought up the Ark from the house of Abinadav in Giv'ah, to bring it to Jerusalem - this is [the meaning of] (II Samuel 6:1) "and David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand." David said, I will not bring up the Ark quietly; immediately he took counsel with the officers of thousands and hundreds, that they send throughout the whole land of Israel, that people gather to them and go to bring it up, as it is said (I Chronicles 13:1) "and David took counsel with the officers of thousands and hundreds, with every leader," etc. And they say further there (II Samuel 6:4) "and Achio walked before the Ark" - from this they said, his brother walked before it. Once they brought it up, ninety thousand elders walked before it, and the priests carried it, and the Levites played music, and all Israel rejoiced - whoever had a lulav [in hand], whoever had a drum or musical instrument - this is [the meaning of] (II Samuel 6:5) "and David and all the house of Israel played before the Lord," etc. - this refers to the lulav, which a person waves.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:44: Further, it says there below (ibid. 14) "and David danced with all his might before the Lord" - come and see how much David demeaned himself for the honor of the Holy One, blessed be He. David could have simply walked before it like a king dressed in his royal garments - but no; rather, he was dressed in beautiful garments in honor of the Ark, and danced before it, as much as can be said, that it is said (I Chronicles 15:27) "and David was clothed with a robe of fine linen, and all the Levites who bore the Ark," etc., for it is written "and David danced with all his might before the Lord" - what is "with all his might"? With all his strength. What is "danced" [mecharker]? That he clapped his hands together and struck [the ground] and said, "Kiri Ram" [an exclamation of joy]; and Israel would shout and blow trumpets and every musical instrument, as it is said (II Samuel 6:15) "and David and all Israel brought up the Ark of the Lord," etc. Once Israel came to Jerusalem, all the women would peer at David from the roofs and windows, and saw him dancing and playing, and it did not concern him - this is [the meaning of] "and it came to pass, as the Ark of the Lord came into the city of David," etc. - here we learn that his wife looked out over him; and from where do we know that all the women of Jerusalem did likewise? Because she says to him (II Samuel 6:20) "how honored the king of Israel was today, who uncovered himself today before the eyes of his servants' maidservants," and "and King David saw... leaping and dancing," etc. - once she saw him making himself like a commoner, he was demeaned in her eyes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:45: Further, they elaborate there on what she said to him, "as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself," and they explain there that this means "the emptiest of the empty ones," for there is none emptier than him in all the commandments. And he answered, "and I will be still more lightly esteemed than this"; and it says there, do not say I was [demeaned] in others' eyes but not in my own - the verse teaches "and will be lowly in my own eyes." "And with the maidservants of whom you spoke, I will be honored" - he said to her, those daughters of Israel, those "maidservants," are not [merely] maidservants but rather mothers [imahot] - would that I have a portion with them in the future to come! This is [the meaning of] "and with the maidservants of whom you spoke" - would that I be honored with them! And because Michal spoke thus, she was punished, for it is written afterward (II Samuel 6:23) "and Michal, daughter of Saul, had no child until the day of her death" - but is it not written (II Samuel 3:5) "Yitre'am, by Eglah, David's wife" [understood as: she "lowed" like a heifer (eglah) and died]? This is what is meant by "until the day of her death" - implying that on the day of her death she did have [a child].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:46: There is no man in Israel who demeaned himself for the mitzvot more than David, for he said before the Lord (Psalms 131:2) "God, my heart was not proud" - at the time Samuel anointed me king, "nor did my eyes look haughty" - at the time I killed Goliath, "nor did I go about with great matters" - at the time they restored me to the kingship, "or things too wondrous for me" - at the time I brought up the Ark - "but I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother" - just as a baby is not ashamed to be exposed before his mother, so I have set my soul before You, that I was not ashamed to demean myself before You for Your honor - "like a weaned child with his mother" [midrashically], like a baby just emerged from his mother's womb, who has no proud spirit about nursing from his mother's breast - so was my soul upon me, that I am not ashamed to learn Torah even from the youngest of Israel. Rabbi Adda bar Chinena said, the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, "you have compared yourself to a weaned child - by your life, just as this baby has no sins, so you have no sins," as it is said (II Samuel 12:13) "the Lord has also removed your sin, you shall not die." From this you learn that a person may not conduct himself with pride before the Omnipresent, but rather must demean himself for His honor.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:47: Rabbi Yehudah HaLevi bar Shalom said: the deeds of the Holy One, blessed be He, are not like the deeds of flesh and blood. Why? A servant employed by flesh and blood has fine clothes, which he wears when he goes out into the marketplace, but when he stands to cook, he removes the fine ones and wears torn and ragged ones; and further, when he scrapes the stoves and the oven, he wears his worst garments. But before the Holy One, blessed be He, at the time a priest scrapes the altar and removes its ashes, he wears his finest garments, as it is said (Leviticus 6:3) "and the priest shall put on his linen garment," etc., for "and he shall remove the ashes" - why so? Rather, to make known that there is no pride before the Omnipresent. So too you find with Elazar, who conducted himself with lowliness before the Omnipresent. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: Elazar was a chief above chiefs and a prince above princes, as it is said (Numbers 3:32) "and the chief of the chiefs of the Levites was Elazar son of Aaron the priest," etc. - see the authority in his hand! And you might think that, because he was a great man, he would give to others the task of carrying the vessels he was appointed to carry, but rather he himself carried them, as it is said (ibid. 4:16) "and the appointed duty of Elazar son of Aaron the priest," etc. And where did he carry all these? Our Sages say, thus he carried them: the oil for the light in his right hand, and the incense of spices in his left, and the daily grain offering hanging from his arm; and the anointing oil, where was it? Rabbi Acha said in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: the vial was like a lentil in size, and he would place it inside his belt-pouch, because he was girded at his waist with it, like a servant before his master, to make known that there is no haughtiness before God. "Appointed duty of the whole Tabernacle and all that is in it, in the sanctuary and its vessels" - for through him he would give them the Ark and the Table and the Menorah and the altars and all their vessels, as it is written "and their charge is the Ark," etc., "and the chief of the chiefs of the Levites, Elazar," etc. - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:48: In the Jerusalem Talmud (Shabbat, chapter 10, halacha 3), they say: one oil in his right hand and one oil in his left, and the incense in his lap and the loaves on his shoulder - such was his lowliness, in accordance with his greatness, to honor the Omnipresent, carrying all this burden at once.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:49: They also say (Keritot 28b) that a certain priest performed the [Temple] service wearing silk gloves on his hands - and the law is that nothing may intervene between his hands and the service - and his punishment was that his hands were cut off by order of the government.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:50: Of this kind of honor is honoring the synagogue and the study hall, since the synagogue is a place where the Shechinah, called "kavod" [glory], rests, as David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 26:8) "I love the habitation of Your house and the place where Your glory dwells"; and so Isaiah the prophet said, concerning the Temple (Isaiah 60:13) "to beautify the place of My sanctuary, and I will make the place of My feet glorious." And it is known that the synagogue is called a "small sanctuary," as our Sages, of blessed memory, explain in Megillah, chapter 3 (29a). Therefore one must honor it and sweep it and remove from it all dust and filth and the like, in the manner that royal palaces are honored; and Sefer Chasidim says (siman 128) concerning Rashi's grandfather, that he would clean, with his beard, the place of the Ark where the Torah scroll was kept.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:51: Further, concerning the synagogue, one should be careful, when leaving it, not to leave with his back to the sanctuary where the Torah scroll is, but rather turn his face toward the Ark; and likewise when stepping down from the platform where the Torah scroll is. This is learned from the sons of Kehat, who did thus when carrying the Ark - their words in the midrash (Bemidbar Rabbah 5:8): and in another matter they were superior to all the Levites - all who carried the rest of the Tabernacle walked in their normal manner, facing the direction they walked, but the sons of Kehat walked backward, with their faces toward the Ark, so as not to turn their backs to the Ark. You thus find that although they were greater than the other families - and certainly than the rest of Israel - they did not become haughty, but were subjugated before the Ark. Why so? Because there is no greatness before God - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:52: Further, concerning the honor of the synagogue - that one not spit in it if possible; and if it is impossible, being that he is naturally so inclined, he should spit discreetly beneath his clothing and rub it in with his feet, and on the Sabbath he should cover it with his feet and not rub it in unless it is a stone floor. Best of all is to have a special cloth to wipe his spittle, so as not to expel spittle from his mouth into the air of the synagogue, and thereby escape the accounting mentioned, "one who spits in front of his fellow and is repulsed by it," for which he is punished, as is explained in the Talmud (Chagigah 5a), and we quoted its words above. And it is likewise the way of kings that not one of their officers spits in his courtyard, how much more so in his house; the general rule for matters of fear is: let the fear of Heaven be upon you like the fear of flesh and blood.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:53: Further, concerning the honor of the synagogue - that one not raise his voice within it to call anyone or the like, since it is the way of those who dwell in a royal palace not to raise their voice before him, but rather to speak in a hushed voice. Behold the testament of the Ramban, peace be upon him, to his son, that he conduct himself in a manner of humility and never raise his voice except in Torah study and prayer, because "the whole earth is full of His glory" - this is part of the way of humility and is fitting to observe always, and how much more so while standing in the house of the King, the King of the world, where His Shechinah dwells, that it is fitting to conduct oneself with this humility; and by this he shows that he has fear of the Shechinah and fulfills the commandment "you shall fear My sanctuary."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:54: The reason fear is obligated toward the sanctuary and holy places is that in every place where there is holiness, one must fear, as we explained above, that our father Jacob, peace be upon him, said concerning this (Genesis 28:17) "and he was afraid and said, how awesome is this place; this is none other than the house of God" - and Onkelos translates, "this is not an ordinary place," etc. This is because it is the way of those who dwell before the king that his fear is upon them, and although His glory, blessed be He, fills the world, out of His love for us He constricted His Shechinah among us, just as He constricted His Shechinah between the poles of the Ark and in the Holy of Holies. Likewise in the Tent of Meeting, we find that once it was completed, it is written (Exodus 40:35) "and Moses could not enter the Tent of Meeting, because the cloud rested upon it, and the glory of the Lord filled the Tabernacle"; and so in the Temple, when Solomon brought the Ark into the Holy of Holies, it is written there (I Kings 8:11) "and the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the Lord filled the house of the Lord"; and so the synagogue is full of the light of the glory of the Lord, and although we do not see anything, we must believe this with complete faith.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:55: It is fitting that we draw an argument from minor to major, to honor the synagogue [more] than the honor we show elders - for the honor of elders is as we have written above, "who sees the supernal, holy beard, and is not ashamed by it"; along these lines, whoever sees the preciousness of the Shechinah, called "kavod," should not be ashamed. And if you say, but it is not seen - then you are lacking in faith; and along these lines it is said in the portion of Va'etchanan (260b), that whoever opens his eyes while reciting the silent Amidah demeans the Shechinah, having no fear of the Shechinah; and from this we learn regarding the other holy matters in the synagogue. We shall elaborate further on the matter of the synagogue in the Gate of Holiness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:56: Just as a person is obligated to conduct himself with honor in the synagogue because of its holiness, so it is fitting to conduct himself with holiness in the study hall, for the law is that the holiness of the study hall exceeds the holiness of the synagogue. And it is likewise fitting to conduct oneself with honor toward the mezuzah, because of the honor of the holiness of the Name within it, and it is explained in the Zohar (Va'etchanan 264a) that one should be careful not to pour dirty water in front of the mezuzah - his words: "and therefore a person must not create filth and dirt at the doorway, and must not pour out dirty water: one reason, so as not to demean the Name of his Master; and another, because that destroyer has permission to destroy [there]. And therefore a person must be careful of this, and a person must be careful and not remove the Name of his Master from the doorway of his house" - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:57: Whoever refrains from honoring the Omnipresent for the sake of the honor of this world is punished, and of him the prophet Isaiah says (Isaiah 10:3) "and what will you do on the day of reckoning, and in the desolation that will come from afar? To whom will you flee for help, and where will you leave your glory?" So too it says in "Margenita of Rabbi Meir," as we quoted its words above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:58: There is another aspect concerning honor: to distance oneself from the honor of this world, for the more a person honors himself, the more the supernal honor flees from him, as it is said (Proverbs 12:9) "better to be lightly esteemed and have a servant," etc. This will be further elaborated in the Gate of Humility.
